cells.tense: You are here with what has not been decided yet, and the openness is all of it now.
cells.act: choose the light to steer by and turn toward it
cells.ask: Name what you'd grieve if it stayed unopened forever, and take a step toward it, no explanation owed to anyone.
cells.core:
You can stand in front of something undecided and not rush it. Nothing is committed yet, and that doesn't scare you — you're just here with it, available, and today's version looks different from yesterday's. That's not a stall. Things stay open around you because you don't grip them shut by naming them too early.

Of everything still unopened here, one of them you'd grieve if it stayed unopened forever. Name that one, and take a step toward it. Not a plan, a step. Take it tomorrow without justifying it to anyone, and let wanting it count as reason enough. Plenty stays undecided longer than you'd like, and people will ask what you're doing. You'll know what the step was for once it's behind you.

cells.verb: standing before anything is chosen, holding it all open
cells.place: where you release what you've been gripping, on purpose, to clear the space

cells.tense: The next version of everything keeps being held open, and none of it is ever going to land.
cells.act: do the thing in your own way, without proving it
cells.ask: Carry out one ordinary task in your own shape this afternoon — let nobody see the reasoning behind it, then or later.
cells.core:
You keep what matters most where it could still become anything, and you guard that. Each version stays more open than the first, so nothing has to be the shape it is yet. From where you stand the guard has a careful feel. From the other side, it's a long stretch of watching with nothing coming out.

There is another half you can try. Carry out one ordinary task today in your own shape, the version you'd normally soften for the room, and let nobody see the reasoning behind it. Don't explain it after. If it feels too plain to be enough, sit with that a minute before softening it. What you kept open gets to be a real thing today, and it will still be there tomorrow.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping everything open instead of letting one thing land.

cells.tense: Something is still standing at a doorway that closed a while back, and the openness hasn't come back through it.
cells.act: look at the same thing longer, until it shows you more
cells.ask: Stay with what you already love well past your usual turning-away point, and carry back whatever shows up that hadn't appeared before.
cells.core:
The openness that was yours has narrowed. Where you used to stand before what could still become anything, you work now from a smaller place — careful, guarded, not quite arriving in what's here. You still care for what you tend. You just don't let it stay unshaped around you anymore, and what you make now comes out of that tightness.

Widening comes back through staying, not through forcing feeling. Stay with something you already love longer than you normally would — until it shows you a thing it hadn't shown you yet. Keep a rough count of what appears, three or five or just one, and bring them along to the next time. Nothing needs deciding about any of it. Staying is what opens the door from your side.

cells.tense: A door is being closed for you right now, and you're at the hinge with the pen down.
cells.act: picture it a year on, turned out well, and keep the picture
cells.ask: See something that matters twelve months ahead, turned out well. Hold the picture with no schedule on it and no telling anyone.
cells.core:
You move by reflex a lot of the time and don't see the options you actually have. When a thing opens, you answer with the first shape that fits, or the one that answers someone else's question, and the fact that you chose it doesn't register anywhere. Doors are there. You walk past them without writing your name on the turn.

A picture will do more here than a plan. Take something that matters, see it twelve months ahead turned out well, and hold the picture — no deadlines, no telling anyone. If it sharpens over a week or two, keep it. If it fades, the thing it was about will show itself differently and you can look again. You are making shape all day long already, often without noticing; this lets you see it in your own hand.
cells.sheetLine: You're making the shape and filing it under circumstance.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person has a specific history of sealed openings, so the Too Little cell must stay with constriction showing up now and not name what caused it. A reader could reasonably say they do let go fine and this is just ordinary patience, so the core leans on what the capacity looks like in a moment, not a verdict. The asks are still useful if the read is wrong: each one teaches something even if this isn't the reader's shape, and none promises a fix. The sentence in the Too Much draft that serves the writer more than the person is 'it feels like generosity' — cut that and keep the guard itself.
